New transit fares from January: what changes and who pays less

By Farah Haddad · Updated 21 October 2026

The city's transport authority has confirmed a new fare structure for buses, trams and the metro, which takes effect on the first Monday in January. Here is what is changing, and what it means for your journeys.

What is changing?

The three fare zones are being replaced by a single flat fare for any journey within the city boundary. A single trip, including any changes made within ninety minutes, will cost 2.10 on a contactless card or the transit app. Paper tickets bought from machines will cost 2.60.

Who pays less?

Anyone who regularly travels across zones will save money. A commuter travelling from the outer suburbs to the centre currently pays 3.80 each way, so the change cuts their daily cost by more than three. People making short trips inside the centre will pay slightly more than today's 1.90.

Selected fares before and after the change
TicketNowFrom January
Single trip, central zone only1.902.10
Single trip, outer suburbs to centre3.802.10
Weekly pass, all zones34.0026.00

Is there a daily cap?

Yes. Contactless and app users will never pay more than 6.30 in a single day, however many trips they make. A weekly cap of 26 replaces the current weekly pass, so there is no need to buy a pass in advance.

What about concessions?

Children under twelve continue to travel free. Students, apprentices and people receiving certain benefits will get half-price fares on the same flat structure. To get the discount, you will need to register your card or app account once:

  1. Create or sign in to an account on the transit app or website.
  2. Upload proof of your student, apprentice or benefit status.
  3. Wait for a confirmation email, which the authority says should take no more than five working days.

Why is this happening?

The authority says the zones were confusing for visitors and unfair to people living in the outer suburbs, who often have the lowest incomes and the longest journeys. It expects the change to cost about 14 million a year in lost revenue, to be made up partly from a new levy on large car parks.
